newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican politician warns of "peso" catastrophe.
newsitem.headline: Mexican politician warns of "peso" catastrophe.

text.p: A leading Mexican opposition politician warned on Tuesday of a new peso "catastrophe" like the one that shook world financial markets in 1994-1995.

Vicente Fox, charismatic governor of the central state of Guanajuato, took out full-page ads in local newspapers charging that the peso was overvalued, as it had been in 1994 before the government devalued the currency and touched off the country's worst economic crisis in 50 years.

"We don't want another economic catastrophe," said Fox, considered a rising star within the conservative National Action Party (PAN). "All examples of overvaluation of our currency have ended in economic catastrophe. We ask the authorities to avoid a new blow to the economy that is already hurting," he said.

After its spectacular crash in late 1994 and early 1995, the peso has gained in real terms against the dollar, helping the economy to begin a recovery. Although it is now freely floating, meaning the market sets its price, economists say it could become artificially overvalued if a lot of foreign money enters Mexico's financial markets, as has been the case in the past few months.

Some economists warn that much of that money is short-term, or "hot," and could leave Mexico at any time, forcing the peso down. In 1994, many investors took their money out of Mexico in search of higher returns elsewhere, which also fuelled the crisis.
Few politicians or economists in Mexico expect a major crisis because the peso is not nearly as strong as in 1994, but the stronger it gets the more serious any market correction would be.
Some, including Fox, fear a stronger peso will hurt Mexican exports, the most dynamic part of the economy.
